question.en: How are SSR and React Server Components different?

answer.en: SSR describes producing initial HTML on a server and then hydrating the client React tree so it becomes interactive. The component code generally participates in both server rendering and client hydration. A Server Component is a different module-graph model: it renders ahead of the client bundle in a server environment, and its component code is not sent to the browser. It can access server-side data and compose with Client Components, while interactive state, Effects, event handlers, and browser APIs belong on the client side. Frameworks such as Next.js combine RSC, SSR, routing, caching, and streaming, but those terms describe different layers.

question.en: If Server Component code never ships to the browser, how does the page stay interactive, and what exactly does the browser receive for those components?

answer.en: The browser receives the rendered output of Server Components as part of the RSC payload, serialized elements describing the tree, not their source code. Interactive parts are Client Components whose code is in the client bundle; they hydrate and take over event handling. Server and Client Components compose into one tree with the boundary at `use client` (https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components).

question.en: What does use client mean in the Next.js App Router?
A file starts with `'use client'`. Does that mean it never runs on a server?

answer.en: No. Client Components are still server-rendered into the initial HTML and then hydrated; the directive marks where the server module graph ends and the client bundle begins. What it changes is which code ships to the browser and which capabilities are allowed below the boundary (state, Effects, event handlers), not where the component can render (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components).

question.en: A Server Component passes `onRefresh={() => reload()}` down to a Client Component. What is wrong, and what are the legal ways across the boundary?

answer.en: Props crossing from server to client must be serializable, and an ordinary function closure is not. The supported crossing is a Server Function marked with `'use server'`, which the framework passes as a callable reference. Alternatives are making the refresh a client-side concern (revalidation from the client) or restructuring so the callback is not needed (https://react.dev/blog/2024/12/05/react-19#server-actions).

question.en: What causes hydration mismatches, and how should you fix them?

answer.en: `hydrateRoot` expects the initial client render to produce the same output as the server HTML. Mismatches commonly come from `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, locale-dependent formatting, browser-only APIs or branches, different request data, invalid HTML nesting, or a changing external data source. Find and remove the nondeterminism or make the same snapshot available to both sides. If content intentionally differs, use a documented two-pass pattern or a narrow suppression escape hatch only when the difference is understood. Hydration warnings are not cosmetic: React cannot guarantee every differing attribute is patched, and event behavior can become incorrect.

question.en: The team silences a timestamp mismatch with `suppressHydrationWarning`. What does that attribute actually do?

answer.en: It suppresses the warning for that element's text content and some attributes, one level deep; it does not reconcile the difference or make the mismatch safe. It is acceptable only for known, unavoidable differences such as a formatted timestamp. The general fix is removing the nondeterminism or using a two-pass pattern that renders the same value on both sides (https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/hydrateRoot).

question.en: Why is `typeof window !== 'undefined' ? <FullWidget /> : null` during render not a fix, even though the warning disappears?

answer.en: It removes the warning by making the server and client first renders agree, but only by rendering nothing on the server: users get no meaningful HTML for that subtree, and hydration still has to replace it. The documented pattern is a two-pass render (render a consistent placeholder, switch after mount via an Effect) or making the same data snapshot available to both sides.

question.en: How would you decide where data fetching belongs in a Next.js App Router tree?

answer.en: Start with ownership and delivery: fetch request-scoped or secret-backed data in a Server Component close to the data source, and keep interactive or browser-dependent fetching in a Client Component or supported client cache. Place the request at the component that needs it so unrelated UI can render or stream independently, while using the framework's documented caching and revalidation controls. Avoid turning a whole route into a Client Component just to support one interactive leaf. For slow or uncached work, put a Suspense boundary near that work. The right placement depends on freshness, authorization, bundle cost, interaction latency, and the desired loading sequence.

question.en: One leaf of a page needs `useState`, so a developer marks the whole page `'use client'` to make the error go away. What did that cost?

answer.en: The page's imports all enter the client bundle, and its data fetching moves to the client side or must be threaded through props, losing server-side data placement close to the source. Every descendant below the boundary becomes client code. The fix is keeping the page a Server Component and pushing `'use client'` down to the interactive leaf, passing serializable props (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components).

question.en: What architectural role do layouts, loading files, and error files play in the App Router?

answer.en: The App Router organizes UI by route segments. Layouts provide persistent shared structure, while a segment's `loading.js` creates a loading boundary around the route content for navigation and streaming. An `error.js` file is a client error boundary for uncaught errors in that segment and can offer a retry operation; errors bubble to the nearest parent boundary. Expected operational failures, such as validation errors, should normally be modeled as returned values rather than thrown into an error boundary. Choose the boundary granularity from the user experience: isolate a widget or segment when the rest of the page should remain usable.

question.en: A fetch in a segment returns a 404-style 'not found' result and the developer throws it so `error.js` shows the message. Why is that the wrong boundary?

answer.en: `error.js` is a client error boundary for uncaught, unexpected errors in a segment. A missing record is an expected operational outcome: model it as a returned value and a rendered state so the surrounding layout stays and the UI responds deliberately. Reserve thrown errors for the unexpected (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/error-handling).

question.en: When `error.js` renders for a segment, what happens to the layout above it, and why does that matter for where you put the file?

answer.en: The layout above the failing segment stays on screen; only the segment's content is replaced by the error UI, and errors bubble to the nearest parent boundary. Boundary placement is therefore a product decision: a boundary around one widget keeps the rest of the page usable, while a route-level boundary takes the whole content area down.

question.en: What does Suspense do, and what does it not do?

answer.en:
Suspense defines a UI boundary that can show a fallback while supported work is not ready. Current React integrations include lazy component code, reading a cached Promise with `use`, Suspense-enabled frameworks, and streaming server rendering. When the work resolves, React reveals the children. Suspense does not automatically detect a fetch started in an Effect or event handler, choose cache freshness, or make an arbitrary Promise safe to create during render. A boundary is also a product decision: its fallback should represent a coherent loading unit. Use nested boundaries when parts should reveal independently rather than wrapping every component in a spinner.

```tsx caption="The boundary coordinates the loading experience; the resource activates it."
<Suspense fallback={<ResultsSkeleton />}>
  <SearchResults promise={resultsPromise} />
</Suspense>
```

question.en: A developer wraps a component that fetches inside `useEffect` in `<Suspense>` and expects a spinner. Why does nothing happen?

answer.en: A Suspense boundary is only activated by Suspense-aware work: lazy component loading, reading a cached Promise with `use`, or a Suspense-enabled framework source. A fetch started in an Effect runs after commit and is invisible to the boundary; it manages its own loading state. The fix is a Suspense-enabled data source, not another boundary (https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense).

question.en: How do Suspense and streaming improve a server-rendered page?

answer.en: A streaming renderer can send the static shell and Suspense fallbacks before every async subtree is ready, then send each completed boundary later. The browser can display the shell progressively, and the streamed content replaces its fallback as it arrives. In Next.js App Router, route segments and Suspense boundaries provide the chunks, while the RSC payload lets the client reconcile the component tree and hydrate Client Components. Boundary placement controls the user-visible sequence and the amount of work that can proceed independently. Streaming does not make the response status mutable after bytes have been sent, so classify early errors before streaming when an HTTP error status matters.

question.en: Mid-stream, a subtree throws and the team wants to change the response to 500. Why can't they?

answer.en: The response status and headers are sent with the first flushed bytes, the shell. Once streaming has begun the status is committed; later errors can only be handled inside the stream, as error boundary fallbacks in the HTML. Work whose failure should determine an HTTP error status must complete or fail before the shell is sent (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/streaming).

question.en: Why must a Promise passed to use in a Client Component be cached?

answer.en: A component that suspends may be retried from the beginning. If it creates a fresh Promise during every render, each retry sees a different pending resource and can suspend forever or repeatedly show the fallback. The Promise must come from a cache, a Suspense-enabled framework, an event or route loader, or a Server Component so the same instance is reused for the same resource identity. Cache invalidation should deliberately produce a new Promise, usually as part of a transition or framework revalidation. Do not inspect Promise internals to bypass `use`; let React coordinate resolution and rejection through Suspense and Error Boundaries.

question.en: A Client Component does `const data = use(fetch(url))` inline in render. Describe what the user actually experiences.

answer.en: React does not preserve state for renders that suspended before mounting, so it retries rendering from scratch, and each retry creates a new pending Promise. `use` never observes a resolved instance: React warns about an uncached promise and the fallback shows repeatedly, so content never appears. The Promise must come from a cache, a Suspense-enabled framework, or a Server Component so the same instance is reused (https://react.dev/reference/react/use#caching-promises-for-client-components).

question.en: How do useTransition and useDeferredValue differ?
Does wrapping an update in `startTransition` make the slow render cheaper?

answer.en: No. A transition marks the update as non-urgent so React can keep showing the previous UI and stay responsive to input while preparing the new tree, interrupting the non-urgent work if something urgent arrives. The same work still happens; it is scheduling, not optimization. If the render is too slow, the fix is less work (memoization, splitting, smaller subtrees), not a transition (https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition).

question.en: You control the input in one component and the slow results list in a sibling. Which API fits, and why?

answer.en: The input's owner owns the update decision, so `useTransition` there marks the query-state change as non-urgent and exposes `isPending`. If the slow component only receives a value it does not set, `useDeferredValue` inside it defers the value it renders with, letting the urgent input update land first. The producer marks the update; the consumer defers the value it receives.

question.en: Walk through the core building blocks of an Angular application.

answer.en: Components own a template and a class and split the UI into encapsulated parts. Services hold logic and state shared across components, wired through dependency injection: you declare a dependency and the injector provides it, with hierarchical injectors scoping instances to a component subtree. Templates bind class state to the DOM, with directives for behavior and pipes for formatting. Modern Angular builds on standalone components — no NgModule required — and lazy loading at the route level. Know the vocabulary (component, service, DI, template, standalone vs NgModule): interviews ask you to read Angular code and place yourself in its structure.

question.en: Is dependency injection just a global singleton registry?

answer.en: No: injectors are hierarchical, so a component subtree can own its own instance and lifetime.

question.en: How do change detection and signals work in modern Angular?

answer.en: Change detection decides when a template re-renders. Historically Zone.js patched async APIs and marked the app dirty on any event; modern Angular tracks state usage granularly with signals — a wrapper around a value that notifies consumers on change — and updates only the templates that read the changed signal. computed derives lazily and memoizes from other signals; effect runs side effects against non-reactive APIs; OnPush components render only when their inputs or signals change. Reactive context is synchronous: a signal read after an await is not tracked, so read signals before the async boundary. RxJS interop exists (async pipe, toSignal), but the mental model is: signals for synchronous state, observables for event streams.

question.en: A signal read after an await still updates the template, right?

answer.en: No: reactive context is synchronous; reads after an async boundary are not tracked. Read signals before the await.
